newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo banks seek more balanced monetary policy.
newsitem.headline: Yugo banks seek more balanced monetary policy.

text.p: The Association of Yugoslav banks (YBA) supported late on Wednesday the central bank's efforts to tighten monetary stance but also asked for a more selective approach in closing down insolvent banks.
Bankers insisted the ailing banking sector was a reflection of the entire economy and their own business strategy, said the statement published in Belgrade daily Politika on Thursday.

Emphasizing the need for rehabilitation and restructuring of the banking system, YBA asked the National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) to offer commercial banks a relief by clearing their balances of old hard currency savings and external debt.
It is inevitable to rehabilitate big loss-making banks, before any restructuring begins, YBA said in its statement.
YBA's Board of Directors meeting was attended by top central bank officials, who reiterated the NBY's commitment to restrictive monetary policy.
According to the statement, NBY will continue to apply currency board mechanism and issue only as many dinars as backed by the hard currency equivalent.
In future, loans extended for liquidity purposes will have to be collateralized by hard currency.
NBY officials said it would prevent any increase in the banks' lending activity.

Only those banks which collected payments on previously extended credits will be able to use those funds for further lending activity. The credit potential volume will be frozen at the level of December 31, 1996, the statement said.
YBA also called for rescheduling credits which the central bank extended via commercial banks to exporters.
Rescheduling period was yet to be decided, a member of the YBA Board of Directors told Reuters.
"Bankers are only trying to put down the fire, but they are not acting upon the cause," said an analyst who spoke under condition of annonymity.

"If one insolvent bank is closed, mistrust grows and the crisis spreads like a domino effect. People go to another bank, try to protect themselves by withdrawing deposits. Such behaviour puts pressure on other banks and the problem grows." -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
